summary: Energy first, water derived from it. Per-prompt energy comes from 2025 vendor disclosures (OpenAI ~0.34 Wh, Google median 0.24 Wh for text); water = energy x water intensity. 'onsite' counts data-centre cooling only; 'comprehensive' adds the water consumed generating the electricity.

usage_tiers.mixed: Mixed – text plus some images and reasoning

boundaries.onsite: Vendor-reported, onsite data-centre cooling only (~1 mL/Wh, implied by Google's 2025 disclosure)
boundaries.comprehensive: Onsite cooling plus water consumed generating the electricity (~4.1 mL/Wh; US grid average per Li et al.)

why_estimates_vary_100x: When it was measured: Google reports a 33x drop in energy per prompt in twelve months; 2023 estimates (~40 mL/prompt) describe hardware that no longer exists.

Where the line is drawn: onsite cooling only vs including water used to generate the electricity gives figures several times apart. Neither is wrong; a figure that does not say which cannot be checked.
What is measured: chat prompts vs agentic tasks, which reprocess a growing context over dozens of calls and can exceed per-prompt figures by orders of magnitude.
Whose data centre: onsite water intensity differs ~9x between providers – 0.12 L/kWh (Amazon), 0.27 (Microsoft), ~1.08 implied by Google. This methodology uses the highest.
limitations: Vendor figures are not peer-reviewed, describe median prompts and exclude model training.
Electricity-generation water uses US grid averages; real figures depend on data-centre location and grid mix.
Results are indicative estimates, not measurements.

sources.name: Google (2025), Measuring the environmental impact of AI inference
sources.used_for: Median Gemini text prompt 0.24 Wh; onsite water 0.26 mL per prompt (~1.08 mL/Wh)

sources.name: OpenAI per-query figures (2025), via DatacenterDynamics
sources.used_for: ~0.34 Wh per ChatGPT query – the 'simple' tier

sources.name: Li et al., Making AI Less Thirsty
sources.used_for: ~3.1 mL/Wh for water consumed in electricity generation (US grid average)

sources.name: MIT Technology Review (2025) analysis
sources.used_for: Image generation and long reasoning at roughly 3 Wh or more – the 'intensive' tier
